- node_network_delay / node_network_packet_loss (node-scoped)
- pod_network_delay (affected pod)
- cpu overload / etc.

L3 branch 3: "The same latency / packet anomaly across every pod on one node → node-scope network fault". But here the drops are across pods on ALL nodes (worker-01, 02, 03). Hmm, unless the drops are on those services that live on one specific node. Let's map:

Drops listed for: ts-auth (w02), ts-basic (w01), ts-cancel (w02), ts-config (w03), ts-contacts (w01), ts-delivery (w02), ts-food (w02), ts-gateway (w03), ts-inside-payment (w01), ts-order (w01), ts-payment (w02), ts-preserve (w03), ts-price (w02), ts-route (w01), ts-seat (w03), ts-security (w02), ts-station (w01), ts-train (w02), ts-travel (w01), ts-ui-dashboard (w03), ts-user (w03).

Spread across all nodes. So node-scope doesn't fit a single node. Hmm.

Unless... the alert list is the ripple, and the real case is a single service with the biggest deviation. The L3 says "read the percentages literally, the case's own number usually dwarfs its callers' rises (ripples come as consequences, never larger than the source)". Here the max are: ts-inside-payment -66.3%/-65.7%, ts-ui-dashboard -64.9%/-63.3%, ts-station -60%, ts-travel -65.7% RPS, ts-gateway -78% RPS, ts-cancel -73.7% RPS, ts-user -67.6% RPS, ts-route -64.8%, ts-order -61.4%...

Nothing dwarfs. All uniform ~-50 to -65%. So there's no single epicenter in the traffic metrics. That's characteristic of the whole namespace's inbound traffic being reduced — e.g., the load generator path. Hmm.

But wait — maybe the anomaly is elsewhere: note the LATENCY_MISSING on ts-payment-service: "Metrics dropped to zero/NaN after injection". Interesting: "after injection" — meaning the fault injection. LATENCY_MISSING means latency metrics missing — that suggests ts-payment-service's metrics stopped (pod dead? no traffic?). And ts-payment inbound dropped -42.8, RPS not given.

Hmm, but ts-payment isn't unique.

Let me reconsider: maybe there's a more targeted signal. The uniform traffic drop across the whole namespace with no latency rise could mean: the front door (ts-ui-dashboard / ts-gateway) can't accept traffic → all downstream drops ~ proportionally. ts-ui-dashboard inbound -64.9%: it's the entry (from ingress/loadgen). Its drop is the largest among "source" nodes alongside inside-payment.

Hmm, but is there another possibility: a node-scope fault on one node where the gateway pod... no, gateway is on w03, and drops happen everywhere.

Consider node fault on worker-03: pods on w03: ts-assurance, ts-config, ts-food-delivery, ts-gateway, ts-news, ts-preserve, ts-seat, ts-ui-dashboard, ts-user, ts-voucher, ts-wait-order, nacos-2, nacosdb-mysql-2, tsdb-mysql-2. The alerts include ts-config, ts-gateway, ts-preserve, ts-seat, ts-ui-dashboard, ts-user — but not ts-assurance, ts-avatar(w02), ts-news, ts-wait-order, ts-voucher, ts-food-delivery. Hmm, ts-assurance, ts-news, ts-voucher, ts-wait-order, ts-food-delivery have no alerts at all. So it's not node-scoped either — services without alerts are spread across nodes.

Actually, no-alert services: ts-assurance (w03), ts-avatar (w02), ts-consign-price (w02), ts-consign (w02), ts-execute (w02), ts-food-delivery (w03), ts-news (w03), ts-notification (w01), ts-order-other (w02), ts-preserve-other (w01), ts-rebook (w01), ts-route-plan (w01), ts-station-food (w01), ts-ticket-office (w01), ts-train-food (w02), ts-travel-plan (w02), ts-travel2 (w01), ts-verification-code (w01), ts-voucher (w03), ts-wait-order (w03). Hmm, so the alert set = services that had traffic. The universal ~50% drop suggests the entry point (load generator → ts-ui-dashboard / gateway) received half traffic. Hmm, or the whole system's throughput halved due to a bottleneck somewhere in the middle.

Actually wait. Let's reconsider the L3 branch: "A constant delay riding on one service's own latency — its p50/p90 jump by a fixed amount, its callers see the same added delay... → pod_network_delay". Here there are no latency alerts — but maybe latency metrics are only available for some services. The ts-payment LATENCY_MISSING is a hint: p90 latency metrics dropped to zero/NaN. That means payment's latency metric stopped being reported — could be because ts-payment-service pod is not reachable/metrics gone.

Hmm, but the incident fault: which service is the "epicenter"? Let me check logs/connectivity. Actually, maybe better: look at the service dependencies and check connectivity for suspect services. Also, we could look at whether there's an obvious one: L3 says the case is the primary anomaly — "carrying the runaway deviation: read the percentages literally, the case's own number usually dwarfs its callers' rises".

Hmm, all percentages are similar magnitude. But hold on: maybe the direction matters: a *drop* propagated downstream from the caller. If a service at the top of the call graph lost inbound traffic (because it's broken), the callers get less traffic. Actually a drop in a provider wouldn't reduce the caller's traffic; a drop in the caller reduces provider traffic. So the epicenter of a *drop* is the top: ts-ui-dashboard / ts-gateway (entry). Actually, if ts-gateway is broken, then downstream services see fewer requests, and ts-ui-dashboard (which calls the gateway) sees fewer outbound and inbound falls too.

The drop magnitudes: ts-ui-dashboard -64.9% inbound, ts-gateway -57.5%, ts-order -57.6%, ts-inside-payment -66.3%. Hmm, ts-ui-dashboard is the entry with the biggest. But that pattern could also arise from a load generator change.

Alternatively the incident could be a traffic-independent fault: e.g., namespace pod quota, deployment zero replicas... no, pods are running.

Let me check events (namespace) — the L3 says object layer is exclusion evidence. Also check service endpoints. But first, maybe there's something else: pod ages all 14m — meaning all deployments rolled out 14 min ago. That's odd: a full rollout of everything 14 minutes before? Maybe the environment was just redeployed; the fault injection happened within that. ts-ui-dashboard restarted 3 times (14m ago).

Hmm, note the alert time range 22:10:28–22:12:18 — a 2-minute window. If pods are 14m old and the current time is ~22:12, then pods started ~21:58.

Let me look for the mechanism: check ts-payment-service logs and the ui-dashboard logs, plus namespace events.

Actually, a smarter approach: run connectivity checks for a few services to find the broken edge, and read error logs. Given the whole namespace shows a traffic drop, one strong candidate in List A for a system-wide effect: "namespace_cpu_quota_exceeded", "namespace_memory_quota_exceeded", "namespace_pod_quota_exceeded". If a namespace ResourceQuota is hit, new pods fail... but everything is running.

Alternatively "node_network_packet_loss" or "node_network_delay" on a node hosting the gateway → all traffic through gateway degrades → global drop with latency... but no latency alert.

Hmm — actually "Network Drop" pps drop is a *packet rate* reduction, which correlates with fewer requests being served. If a node had packet loss, we'd expect latency alerts an
